visuals.title: Quiz
visuals.text: Five questions. Answer along on the cards below the transcript, then hear Marco's answers.

quiz.pause_at: Pause here if you want to think it through

questions.q: A fund buys Harbour for 1,000, with 600 of debt. Five years later it sells for 1,300, with 300 of debt left. What multiple of its money does the fund make?
questions.explain: 1,300 − 300 of debt leaves 1,000 for the equity, on 400 put in: 2.5x. Dividing 1,300 by 400 forgets the debt; 1.3x is the business, not the equity.
questions.explain_at: Two and a half times its money in five years

questions.q: In a leveraged buyout, who owes the acquisition debt?

options.text: The private equity firm that runs the fund
The investors in the private equity fund
The company being bought, through its bidco
The fund and the company, jointly

questions.explain: The bidco borrows and buys the target, so the debt sits with the company and its cash repays it. The fund can lose its equity, but the lenders can't come after it for more.
questions.explain_at: First trap. The fund doesn't owe it

questions.q: What do lenders most want to see in an LBO target?

options.text: Steady cash flows that can carry the debt
Fast growth, so there's plenty of upside
A high multiple that proves its quality
A share price well below its peak

questions.explain: The debt is paid from the company's cash. Fast growth, Sofia's answer, usually eats cash, so a mature business with predictable cash flows suits lenders better.
questions.explain_at: Growth helps, but fast growth usually eats cash

questions.q: Why did RJR Nabisco's board choose KKR's $109 over management's $112?

options.text: KKR's bid used less borrowed money
KKR's bid was worth more in cash
The board wanted management to stay
KKR's offer was more certain

questions.explain: Management's bid had no reset on its securities, so its $112 might have been worth less. Directors were also uneasy about Johnson's golden parachute.
questions.explain_at: The board judged its offer more certain

questions.q: Ember pays about £505m for Ashtead's shares, and Ashtead's net debt is about £117m. Roughly what is the enterprise value?

options.text: About £390m
About £620m
About £505m
About £740m

questions.explain: Enterprise value is equity value plus net debt: £505m + £117m ≈ £620m. Subtracting the debt gives £390m; £505m is the equity alone.
questions.explain_at: Add that and you get an enterprise value of roughly six hundred and twenty million
